entries.name: Gardens of Versailles
entries.purpose: royal display garden of Louis XIV; the built argument of absolutism - nature ordered by the Sun King's will
parts: Le Notre axis from the palace terrace
layout: a single 3.5 km central axis from the palace westward to the Apollo fountain and Grand Canal
symmetrical parterres and groves flanking the axis
the main view is from the palace; paths are secondary to the sightline
entries.found: one, at Versailles west of Paris, France
entries.notes: 800 ha overall, but the famous formal garden is only about 100 ha; model the axis, not the acreage. 55 fountains and 620 jets run only for special fountain shows; the Grand Canal reads from the air as a huge cross.

entries.name: Vaux-le-Vicomte
entries.purpose: private baroque showpiece of Nicolas Fouquet, the king's finance minister; prototype of the jardin a la francaise
parts: Le Vau chassis (the house) with Le Brun ceilings
Grand Canal (about 1 km hidden from the first view)
layout: one long central axis from house to canal, with swelling and hidden depth
parterres closest to the house, then lawn, then hidden canal
everything angled for one long accelerated perspective
entries.found: one, near Melun southeast of Paris, France
entries.notes: The 17 August 1661 fete here outshone the king; Fouquet was arrested three weeks later and Le Vau, Le Notre and Le Brun were set to work at Versailles. Visitors today come for the anamorphosis - a forced-perspective garden that only makes sense from the grand staircase.

entries.name: Villa d'Este
entries.purpose: cardinal's pleasure garden; the Renaissance marvel-garden (giardino delle meraviglie) that taught all later European water gardens
parts: central axis of terraces uphill from the palace
layout: steep terraced hillside behind the palace, crossed by a central axis
water is the whole point - gravity-fed from the Aniene river, no pumps
long walks parallel to the axis link cross-axes of fountains
entries.found: one, at Tivoli east of Rome, Italy
entries.notes: About 4.5 ha with 51 fountains and hundreds of jets, all gravity-powered. UNESCO since 2001; the water engineering is the spectacle, so a voxel build must read as cascading water at every terrace.

entries.name: Boboli Gardens
entries.purpose: Medici family pleasure ground and outdoor sculpture museum behind the Pitti Palace
parts: amphitheatre behind the palace (with Boboli obelisk)
layout: a hillside behind the Pitti Palace cut into terraces
main axis from palace amphitheatre up to Neptune fountain
perpendicular cypress avenue leading to the Isolotto
entries.found: one, behind the Palazzo Pitti in Florence, Italy
entries.notes: 45,000 m2, laid out by Tribolo (died 1550), continued by Ammannati and Buontalenti. The classic Italian Renaissance garden prototype; the grotto and the amphitheatre are its two setpieces.

entries.name: Generalife (Nasrid summer palace gardens)
entries.purpose: royal almunia (farm-villa) and summer retreat of the Nasrid emirs of Granada
parts: Patio de la Acequia (long courtyard with central water channel)
Escalera del Agua (staircase with water channels on the handrails)
Patio del Cipres de la Sultana
layout: terraced hillside above the Alhambra's ravine, in three long 35 x 250 m terraces
water runs in straight channels flanked by hedges - the Islamic charbagh logic on a hillside
seen from the Alhambra across the Cuesta de los Chinos
entries.found: one, above Granada, Spain
entries.notes: Built by Muhammad II (r. 1273-1302), remodelled by Isma'il I in 1319. UNESCO 1984 with the Alhambra. One of the oldest surviving Islamic gardens; the Patio de la Acequia is the scene to model.

entries.name: Fin Garden (Bagh-e Fin)
entries.purpose: Safavid royal retreat; the classic desert qanat garden - green as defiance in the Kashan desert
layout: rectangular walled garden, divided by water channels into four (charbagh)
central pool with a two-storey pavilion
channels run in a strict grid; the water is the wealth on display
entries.found: one, near Kashan, Iran
entries.notes: About 2.3 ha, entirely gravity and qanat fed from springs at the foot of the mountains. UNESCO 2011; oldest extant Persian garden. Amir Kabir, Naser al-Din Shah's chancellor, was assassinated here in 1852.

entries.name: Gardens of Pasargadae (Cyrus the Great)
entries.purpose: royal park of Cyrus II; the first recorded formal garden, the ancestor of every walled paradise garden
parts: Palace P (with fixed throne overlooking the garden)
two rectangular garden plots divided by stone water channels
four quadrant plots (about 70 x 50 m each)
stone channels 25 cm wide with deep square basins every 13-14 m
layout: two large rectangular plots along a long axis below Palace P
channels flush with the ground, basins stepping down across the plain
the throne's sightline bisects the plots - the garden as imperial theatre
entries.found: one set of ruins, at Pasargadae (near modern Shiraz), Iran
entries.notes: The word 'paradise' (Greek paradeisos) comes from this garden - Avestan 'pairidaēza', walled around. UNESCO 2004; the channels are the only surviving hardscape and are the thing to model.

entries.name: Shalamar Gardens, Lahore
entries.purpose: imperial charbagh garden-palace for Emperor Shah Jahan; public spectacle and court entertainment
parts: three terraces (Farah Baksh, Faiz Baksh, divided garden)
layout: a 658 x 258 m walled rectangle, three terraces stepping 4-5 m each
central axis of fountains and cascades
square terrace quadrants divided by long fountain-lined walks
entries.found: one, at Baghbanpura near Lahore, Pakistan
entries.notes: UNESCO 1981 with Lahore Fort. The most waterworks-dense Mughal garden; Lahore's blistering summers are the reason every terrace is engineered for cooling fountains.

entries.name: Humble Administrator's Garden (Zhuozheng Yuan)
entries.purpose: private scholar-official's retirement garden; the archetype of the Suzhou scholar garden
parts: central pond (one third of the site is water)
48 buildings of Ming and later construction
Surging Wave Pond with three islands
layout: composition around one great pond, divided into three sections with separate moods
view always breaks at a corner or through a moon gate to the next scene
Borrowed views of North Temple Pagoda beyond the walls
entries.found: one, Suzhou, Jiangsu, China
entries.notes: 5.2 ha, the largest Suzhou classical garden; built by Wang Xianchen (1509-1526), UNESCO 1997. Water, rocks, architecture and plants - model it as layered views, not as a lawn.

entries.name: Lingering Garden (Liu Yuan)
entries.purpose: private villa garden; celebrated for its artificial mountain and the wordplay of its name
parts: meandering corridors and patterned lattice windows
layout: single scenic circuit around a central pond and its islands
corridors and gateways frame each view like a hanging scroll
the artificial mountain anchors the southeast corner
entries.found: one, Suzhou, Jiangsu, China
entries.notes: 2.33 ha. UNESCO 1997 as part of the Classical Gardens of Suzhou. The name is from Ouyang Xiu's poem - to linger is to forget to go home; the tour path is deliberately hard to leave.

entries.name: Yu Garden (Shanghai)
entries.purpose: private garden built by a Ming official for his father's retirement, now the surviving Ming core of the Shanghai old town
parts: Grand Rockery (12 m of huangshi stone)
dragon walls closing the six sections
layout: six garden sections around a central rockery-and-pond complex
dragon walls divide sections; roof ridge spined like a dragon's back
kitchen garden scale - compact, dense, layered, 'imagining the big from the small'
entries.found: one, beside the Yuyuan bazaar in Shanghai, China
entries.notes: About 2 ha, built by Pan Yunduan. Known as the 'crown of gardens in the southeast'; the most visited Ming garden in China and the densest rockery per square metre.

entries.name: Summer Palace (Yiheyuan)
entries.purpose: Qing imperial summer retreat; the greatest surviving imperial landscape garden in China
parts: Kunming Lake (about 220 ha, three quarters of the site)
Longevity Hill (about 60 m, built from lake spoil)
Long Corridor (728 m of painted beams)
layout: one artificial mountain and one artificial lake - the whole site is an earthwork
west shore causeway copied from Hangzhou's West Lake Su Causeway
Long Corridor links the halls along the front of the hill
entries.found: one, in the western suburbs of Beijing, China
entries.notes: About 290-300 ha, modelled on the West Lake. Sacked by the Anglo-French army in 1860 and again in 1900; Cixi rebuilt it (1886-95) from funds diverted from the fleet - the most famous embezzlement in garden history. UNESCO 1998.

entries.name: Ryoan-ji rock garden (karesansui)
entries.purpose: zen dry-landscape garden for meditation; viewed from the abbot's (hojo) veranda, never entered
layout: a flat rectangle seen only from one side - from the veranda
asymmetric cluster composition; one stone is always hidden from view
raked gravel as water; stones as islands
entries.found: one, inside Ryoan-ji temple, Kyoto, Japan
entries.notes: Only 14 stones visible from any single veranda position - the 15th is never seen. Raked daily by monks. UNESCO 1994; the simplest great garden in the world and the hardest to get right.

entries.name: Kenroku-en
entries.purpose: daimyo stroll garden of the Maeda lords of Kaga; one of Japan's three great gardens
parts: Kotoji stone lantern (two-legged, icon of Kanazawa)
yukitsuri snow rope cones on pines from November
layout: kaiyu-shiki (stroll) garden around the central pond
six attributes named in its name - spaciousness, seclusion, artifice, antiquity, abundant water, broad views
seasonal views staged along the circuit: plum, cherry, azalea, maple, snow
entries.found: one, Kanazawa, Japan
entries.notes: 11.7 ha, built by the Maeda clan from 1676, opened to the public 1874. Special Place of Scenic Beauty. The yukitsuri snow ropes appear in the first snow of November - that single image sells the whole garden.

entries.name: Katsura Imperial Villa (Katsura Rikyu)
entries.purpose: imperial retreat for moon-viewing, poetry and tea; the supreme achievement of Japanese garden art
parts: chisen kaiyu (pond-stroll) circuit around the main pond
shoin buildings in sukiya style (old, middle, new halls)
layout: a pond with three islands threaded by a winding circuit path
borrowed scenery of the Katsura river and western hills
sequence of tiny tea houses revealed one view at a time
entries.found: one, southwest Kyoto, Japan
entries.notes: About 6.9 ha; completed by Prince Toshitada by 1662. Admired by Taut, Gropius and Kahn as proto-modernism - the model for restraint, rough timber and asymmetry. Access only by pre-booked Imperial Household Agency tours.

entries.name: Stourhead
entries.purpose: English landscape garden of the highest order; a man-made Arcadia painted in Claude Lorrain's light
parts: triangular lake dammed from the Stour
Alfred's Tower (30 m, on the hill above)
layout: a circuit walk around an artificial lake dammed into a triangle
each stopsite frames the next like a Claude painting - temple, lake, hill
ha-ha hides the park wall so the estate runs to the horizon
entries.found: one, near Mere in Wiltshire, England
entries.notes: Laid out by Henry Hoare II from 1741; National Trust since 1946. The model landscape garden for half of Europe and the plain proof that English gardens were composed images, not nature.

entries.name: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew
entries.purpose: national botanical research garden and imperial plant distribution hub; science first, spectacle second
parts: Temperate House (1863-99, largest surviving Victorian glasshouse)
layout: layers of design from three centuries on one flat site - Bridgeman, Kent, Chambers, Brown, Nesfield
a picturesque parkland plan overlaid with glasshouse setpieces
layout reads as 18th-century park with Victorian science sheds dropped in
entries.found: one, on the Thames at Kew/Richmond, England
entries.notes: Founded by Princess Augusta in 1759; 132 ha; UNESCO 2003. Every rubber, coffee and cinchona plant in the empire passed through Kew - a garden that ran the botanical economy of the world.

entries.name: Sissinghurst Castle Garden
entries.purpose: English garden of the 20th century's leading poet; the garden-room style made famous
parts: White Garden (the most imitated single bed in England)
layout: a series of hedged 'garden rooms' on a long axis - never the whole garden at once
over-the-wall views tease the next room from every one
axial spine with terminating setpiece (the Tower)
entries.found: one, near Cranbrook in Kent, England
entries.notes: Created by Vita Sackville-West and Harold Nicolson from 1930; about 2 ha of formal garden within a 180 ha estate; National Trust 1967. The White Garden is the modern cottage-garden cipher - model it and plant with restraint.

entries.name: Monet's garden at Giverny
entries.purpose: working artist's garden; the subject of the Water Lilies series and the Orangerie Grandes Decorations
parts: Clos Normand (formal flower garden with central allée)
underpass below the railway line linking the two gardens
layout: two halves split by road and rail - Clos Normand by the house, water garden across the track
Clos Normand is straight allées; water garden is all curves
painted views are composed from the bridge, the banks and the allée
entries.found: one, Giverny in Normandy, France
entries.notes: Monet lived here 1883-1926; about 1 ha of garden; public since 1980 (Fondation Claude Monet). The pond was dug in 1893 from a diverted stream; the bridge is in every water-lily painting - model the bridge, the wisteria and the lilies.

entries.name: Keukenhof
materials: 7 million bulbs planted every autumn (about 1,600 varieties)
entries.purpose: the world's largest bulb display garden; a living catalogue of the Dutch flower-bulb trade
parts: themed show beds (about 100 garden designs replanted yearly)
Keukenhof castle (15th century 'kitchen garden' of the estate)
layout: eight weeks of spring display inside a 19th-century English landscape park
large colour-blocked beds along canals
park walks connect set pieces; the bulb fields outside the fence are the backdrop
entries.found: one, Lisse in the Duin- en Bollenstreek, Netherlands
entries.notes: 32 ha inside a 250 ha estate; opened to the public 1950; about 1.4 million visitors in eight weeks. Open only mid-March to mid-May - a garden that exists only in spring.

entries.name: Birkenhead Park
entries.purpose: the world's first publicly funded municipal park - built with public money, free to everyone
layout: a perimeter ring of drives around open meadow and two winding lakes
Paxton's naturalistic 'English' style - no axial geometry
enclosed by villa plots whose sale paid for the park
entries.found: one, Birkenhead (Wirral), England
entries.notes: Opened 5 April 1847; about 50 ha public inside a 90 ha purchase. Olmsted visited in 1850, called it magnificent, and copied it at Central Park - every public park on Earth descends from this one.

entries.name: Central Park
entries.purpose: democratic green refuge for all classes of Manhattan; the American urban park as social instrument
layout: 4 km x 0.8 km rectangle (341 ha, 843 acres) between 59th and 110th Streets
four transverse roads sunk 2.5 m below grade
picturesque English landscape sequence: Mall (formal) -> Ramble (wild) -> Meadow (pastoral)
entries.found: one, Manhattan, New York City, USA
entries.notes: 843 acres; Greensward Plan by Olmsted and Vaux (1858), inspired by Birkenhead. Seneca Village (Black property owners) was seized for it - remember the park was cleared for the public it now serves. About 42 million visits a year.

entries.name: Prospect Park
entries.purpose: Brooklyn's Central Park - the same designers' second and more personal masterpiece
parts: Long Meadow (the great pastoral sweep, about 90 acres)
layout: meadow in the west, ravine in the middle, lake in the south - all enclosed by a continuous perimeter drive
no transverse roads - a tighter, purer version of the Central Park idea
designed for Brooklyn's then-rural edge
entries.found: one, Brooklyn, New York City, USA
entries.notes: 526 acres (213 ha); Olmsted and Vaux, 1867-73. Olmsted reportedly called it their best work; the Ravine is the closest thing to old-growth forest left in Brooklyn.

entries.name: Hyde Park
entries.purpose: Royal Park of London opened to the public by Charles I; the nation's front lawn, speaker's rostrum and riot ground
parts: the Serpentine lake (with the Serpentine Bridge, 1826)
Rotten Row (route du roi, first lit highway in England)
layout: a flat royal hunting ground turned common - no formal layout
the Serpentine crosses the middle; park reads as one great open bowl of grass
paths radiate from Hyde Park Corner to Kensington Gardens
entries.found: one, Westminster, London, England
entries.notes: 142 ha; enclosed by Henry VIII as a deer park in 1536, opened to the public in 1637. The Great Exhibition of 1851 stood here (Crystal Palace, later moved to Sydenham). Speakers' Corner is the world's longest-running free-speech forum.

entries.name: The Regent's Park
entries.purpose: Prince Regent's pleasure garden and speculative estate development - a park designed to sell the houses around it
parts: Inner Circle with Queen Mary's Gardens
Regent's Canal along the north edge
layout: two concentric circuits - grand Outer Circle, allée-lined Inner Circle
park and terraces designed as one scheme by Nash (and the Burtons)
parkland framed by stucco terraces; the edge is the architecture
entries.found: one, northwest London, England
entries.notes: 166 ha; opened to the public two days a week in 1835. A Georgian speculation that became London's most complete garden-suburb composition - park, canal, zoo and terraces as one design.

entries.name: Bois de Boulogne
entries.purpose: Napoleon III's great English-landscape park for Paris; built as a social safety valve and imperial stage
parts: Lac Inferieur and Lac Superieur (two artificial lakes)
layout: 8 km of perimeter, 846 ha, all serpentine curves - no axial formality
lakes connected by a cascade, walks curving between them
modelled on Hyde Park - which Napoleon III had admired in London
entries.found: one, between Neuilly and Boulogne, west Paris, France
entries.notes: Laid out by Alphand and Barillet-Deschamps from 1853. Paris's second-largest park; Longchamp hosts the Prix de l'Arc de Triomphe - the garden doubles as the city's racing ground.

entries.name: Parc des Buttes-Chaumont
materials: Temple de la Sibylle (replica of Tivoli)
entries.purpose: Second Empire working-class scenery machine; Paris's most theatrical park built on a rubbish heap of quarried gypsum
parts: island of the Temple de la Sibylle (Davioud, 1866)
layout: a stage set built over a dead gypsum quarry - vertical drama in a flat city
lake at the bottom, island cliff with temple at the centre
winding paths, sudden reveals - the opposite of Versailles' one axis
entries.found: one, in the 19th arrondissement, northeast Paris, France
entries.notes: 25 ha; opened 1 April 1867 for the Exposition Universelle. Former site of the Montfaucon gibbet. Alphand called it 'landscape art on a grand scale'; the cascade runs dry in summer by design.

entries.name: Großer Tiergarten, Berlin
entries.purpose: Berlin's central English-landscape park - a former Electoral hunting ground turned public green lung
parts: Grosser Stern with the Victory Column (moved 1938)
layout: 210 ha of undulating woodland and meadow in the city centre
long oblique axes cut through woods (Lenné, 1818-40s)
axis of the Siegessaule bisects the park east-west
entries.found: one, in Mitte, Berlin, Germany
entries.notes: Founded 1527 as Elector Brandenburg's hunting ground, opened to the public under Frederick the Great, replanted 1949-50 after near-total deforestation for firewood in 1945. Berliners picnic under the Siegessaule.

entries.name: Parque del Buen Retiro
entries.purpose: royal pleasure garden built for Felipe IV; now Madrid's great open-air salon
parts: Estanque Grande with the Alfonso XII monument (1902)
Palacio de Cristal (1887, built for the Philippine exhibition)
the Fallen Angel statue (1840, said to be the only public monument to Lucifer)
layout: a large rectangular royal garden grid with a grand basin at the centre
Parterre (formal) near the palace side, landscape park beyond
long paseos (promenades) connect the gates
entries.found: one, Madrid, Spain
entries.notes: 118 ha; built 1630s under Olivares for Felipe IV; Carlos III admitted the public in 1767; fully municipal since 1868. UNESCO 2021 as part of the Paseo del Prado and Buen Retiro landscape.

entries.name: Phoenix Park
entries.purpose: Europe's largest enclosed urban park; Dublin's royal hunting ground turned public common
parts: Wellington Testimonial (1861, 62 m, largest obelisk in Europe)
Phoenix Monument (1747, actually an eagle, not a phoenix)
layout: a vast walled rectangle, about 707 ha, on the Liffey's bend
a single grand road (Chesterfield Avenue) runs the 4 km length
open meadows in the north, woodlands in the east, institutional estates within
entries.found: one, west of Dublin city centre, Ireland
entries.notes: 707 ha; enclosed by the Duke of Ormonde in 1662 with fallow deer still roaming. The largest enclosed city park in Europe; Phoenix is a corruption of fionn uisce, 'clear water', not the bird.

entries.name: Chapultepec Park (Bosque de Chapultepec)
entries.purpose: the oldest designed landscape in the Americas - Aztec rulers' garden, viceregal palace, modern cultural forest
parts: Nezahualcóyotl's garden and aqueduct for Moctezuma I (c. 1460)
layout: a 686 ha urban forest anchored by a 60 m volcanic bluff
first section around castle and lakes; the rest recent annexes
site of the 1847 battle where the Niños Héroes died
entries.found: one, Mexico City, Mexico
entries.notes: Name means 'at the grasshopper hill'. About 15-20 million visitors a year - often called the most visited urban park on Earth. The ahuehuetes are among the oldest living trees in any city.

entries.name: Stanley Park
materials: old-growth coastal rainforest (Douglas-fir, western red cedar)
entries.purpose: Vancouver's defining urban rainforest peninsula; a near-untouched old-growth forest locked inside a city grid
parts: 9 km Seawall (world's longest uninterrupted waterfront path)
layout: 405 ha peninsula, three-quarters enclosed by harbour and English Bay
seawall rings the coast; forest core is trail-crossed
named for Governor General Lord Stanley, 1888
entries.found: one, Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada
entries.notes: 405 ha; opened 1888 as a 'wild park' - Vancouver deliberately did not clear it. The totem poles are carvings from Haida, Gitxsan and other nations, not local Salish originals. National Historic Site 1988; about 8 million visits a year.

entries.name: Golden Gate Park
materials: reclaimed sand dunes (planted with Monterey pine, cypress, eucalyptus)
entries.purpose: the largest deliberately created landscape in America - 1,000 acres of engineered dunes made into forest
parts: Conservatory of Flowers (1878, oldest existing conservatory in North America)
layout: 4.8 km x 0.8 km rectangle, larger than Central Park
eastern formal portion, western woodland - Hall's two-character plan
windmills at the Pacific end pumped water for irrigation until the 1930s
entries.found: one, San Francisco, California, USA
entries.notes: 1,017 acres (412 ha); reclaimed from shifting sand by William Hammond Hall (from 1871) and John McLaren (superintendent 1890). Olmsted toured in 1886 and praised the transformation.

entries.name: Mount Auburn Cemetery
entries.purpose: America's first rural (garden) cemetery; the precedent for every public park in the United States
layout: winding carriage drives over glacial drumlins - no grid, no straight line
inspired directly by Père Lachaise (Paris, 1804)
arboretum and sanctuary rolled into one design
entries.found: one, Cambridge/Watertown, Massachusetts, USA
entries.notes: 71 ha (175 acres); founded 1831 by the Massachusetts Horticultural Society on Père Lachaise principles. Drew more visitors than Niagara Falls in its first decades - and taught America to build Central Park.

entries.name: Park Güell
entries.purpose: failed bourgeois garden-city turned public park; Gaudí's freest work and Barcelona's most photographed square
parts: serpentine bench (110 m long, longest in the world)
layout: terraced hillside garden-city - 60 lots planned, 2 built
market hall with columns carrying a wavy public square
Gaudí preserved existing trees and carved paths around them
entries.found: one, on Carmel hill, Barcelona, Spain
entries.notes: 17 ha; Eusebi Güell's speculative English garden-city failed in 1914 (2 of 60 houses sold); the city bought it in 1922 and opened it in 1926. UNESCO 1984 with Gaudí's other works.

entries.name: The High Line
materials: peeling white paint and rust (patina kept)
entries.purpose: aerial linear park built on a dead freight railway - the 21st century's most influential urban park typology
parts: Gansevoort St (meatpacking) entry with the Spur
Rail Yards (with Hudson Yards and the Vessel)
layout: 2.33 km of elevated path at about 9 m, Gansevoort to 34th Street
path width varies - plaza, grove, passage, lawn
perspective over Manhattan never leaves you; street below visible through plantings
entries.found: one, Manhattan's West Side, New York City, USA
entries.notes: Opened in stages 2009, 2011, 2014 (Spur 2019); saved by Friends of the High Line (founded 1999) against demolition. Inspired by Paris's Promenade Plantée (1993) and birthed a global wave of rail-yard linear parks.

entries.name: Millennium Park
entries.purpose: billion-dollar civic living room built on a century of rail yards - Chicago's public art engine
layout: 9.9 ha on top of a rail yard and parking deck - every structure is a roof
performance lawn oriented to the city, not away from it
two axes cross at the Bean; everything is seen in relation to skyline
entries.found: one, downtown Chicago, Illinois, USA
entries.notes: Opened July 2004; cost $475M (public-private). At the time the world's largest green roof. Anish Kapoor's Cloud Gate is the single most-photographed public artwork in North America.

entries.name: Gardens by the Bay
materials: supertrees (reinforced concrete core, steel canopy, 25-50 m)
OCBC Skyway (128 m aerial walkway, 22 m high)
entries.purpose: Singapore's 'City in a Garden' proof specimen - a garden the size of a botanical park built on reclaimed swamp
parts: Bay South (54 ha) and Bay East
layout: 101 ha of reclaimed land at Marina Bay, three gardens (South, East, Central)
Supertrees behave as vertical parks - shade, light and irrigation for real plants
the visitor always arrives under the 50 m canopy silhouette
entries.found: one, Marina Bay, Singapore
entries.notes: Opened 29 June 2012; designed by Grant Associates and Gustafson Porter with Wilkinson Eyre as architect. The Supertrees are working technology - rainwater catchment and solar chimneys, not just sculpture.

entries.name: Singapore Botanic Gardens
entries.purpose: the engine of Southeast Asia's rubber economy and the living emblem of the Garden City idea
layout: 82 ha along a 2.5 km north-south spine
English landscape garden plan imposed on a tropical forest
science core at Tanglin, leisure heartland at Symphony Lake
entries.found: one, Tanglin, Singapore
entries.notes: Founded 1859; H.N. Ridley's rubber research here created the Malayan latex boom (1888 onward). First and only tropical botanic garden UNESCO-listed (2015). About 4.5 million visits a year, free except the orchid garden.

entries.name: Ibirapuera Park
entries.purpose: São Paulo's lungs and its quadricentennial monument - the modernist park that anchored Brazil's cultural capital
layout: 158 ha of interlaced building and park - the architecture is the paths
marquise (about 290 m of continuous covered walkway) ties the pavilions together
landscape by Augusto Teixeira Mendes; Burle Marx consulted but was not used
entries.found: one, São Paulo, Brazil
entries.notes: Opened 21 August 1954 for São Paulo's 400th birthday. About 18 million visits a year - the most-visited park in Latin America. Niemeyer's buildings are listed national heritage (IPHAN).
